The biggest kingdom in the archipelago was not destroyed by an enemy from outside.
It fell apart over an inheritance fight inside its own house.
This is the story of the Paregreg War.
After King Hayam Wuruk died in 1389, Majapahit split in two.
The main throne in the Western Palace went to Wikramawardhana, the husband of the crown princess.
In the Eastern Palace ruled Bhre Wirabhumi, the king's son by a concubine.
Each of them believed he deserved the crown more.
In 1404, the tension exploded into the Paregreg War.
The word means a war that comes in stages, back and forth, and wears everyone out.
At first, the Eastern forces had the upper hand, and pushed deep toward the center of Majapahit.
Months turned into years, and the soldiers on both sides grew exhausted.
But Wikramawardhana received fresh troops and turned the tide.
In 1406, the Eastern Palace was attacked in return.
Bhre Wirabhumi lost, and tried to escape by boat at night.
But he was caught and killed.
The Western Palace won.
But it was a hollow victory.
The royal treasury was drained, and the army was shattered.
Worse, in the chaos, Majapahit troops killed one hundred seventy envoys from Ming China, who were visiting.
Ming China demanded a huge fine in gold.
And one by one, the lands Majapahit ruled across the archipelago began to break away.
Since the Paregreg War, the glory of Majapahit never truly recovered,
until it finally collapsed around the fifteen hundreds.
The biggest lesson: however strong a kingdom is, its deadliest enemy often comes from within.
